lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.lesson_title: Variables and Expressions: Read, Write, and Evaluate
lessons.previous_learning: Day 15 percent repair was strong. Atticus correctly repaired unknown-whole and decimal-scale errors and showed mastery across new transfer problems. Percent now moves to short retrieval rather than full-block remediation.
lessons.course_context: Begin a new Grade 6 expressions unit after a five-item percent retrieval check.
learning_objectives: Tell the difference between an expression and an equation.
Write simple expressions from plain-language phrases.
Evaluate expressions by substituting a given value for a variable.
lessons.why_it_matters: Variables let mathematics describe changing quantities and unknown values. This is the language used later in algebra, science, coding, and modeling.

vocabulary.definition: a letter that stands for a number
a math phrase made of numbers, variables, and operations
one part of an expression separated by plus or minus
find the value of an expression
replace a variable with a given number

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: start with five quick percent questions to prove yesterday's repair stuck. If you get at least four correct, move on. A variable is a letter that stands for a number. An expression has no equals sign. To evaluate an expression, replace the variable with the given value and follow the normal order of operations. Keep wording simple: '5 more than n' means n+5; '5 times n' means 5n.

worked_examples.title: Words to expression
worked_examples.problem: Write: 5 more than a number n.
worked_examples.explanation: Start with n and add 5. 5n would mean five times n.

worked_examples.title: Order matters
worked_examples.explanation: Start with x and take away 7. 7-x is a different expression.

worked_examples.title: Real situation
worked_examples.problem: A game gives 10 points per win plus 25 bonus points. Let w be wins.
worked_examples.explanation: 10 points for each win gives 10w, then add 25.

independent_practice.prompt: A streaming game costs $6 per month plus a one-time $15 fee. Write an expression for m months. Then find the cost for 4 months.

exit_ticket.prompt: What is the difference between an expression and an equation?
exit_ticket.answer: An expression has no equals sign; an equation states that two expressions or values are equal.

lessons.voice_prompt: Speak directly to Atticus using short, age-appropriate questions. Begin with the five-item percent retrieval check. If he gets 4/5 or better, congratulate the specific accuracy and move to the new expressions unit. Teach before questioning. Use the whiteboard for DIFFERENT examples to show n+5 versus 5n, x-7 versus 7-x, and substitution boxes for evaluating an expression. Never put assigned final answers on the board. If Atticus asks what a word means, define it in one plain sentence and return to the math.
lessons.teacher_notes: Advance from percent; keep 5-10 minutes of percent retrieval on future days.
